idiom_name: layer interface (declared type) + embedded base struct (shared implementation)
implementation_notes: Go has no type inheritance by design, so the layer's declared type is an interface - satisfied implicitly by every type that implements its methods - while the behavior the layer shares lives in a struct that members embed, whose methods are promoted to the embedding type. Embedding is composition, not subclassing: promotion is resolved at compile time, the outer type is not a subtype of the embedded one, and redeclaring a method on the outer type shadows the promoted version instead of overriding it dynamically. Use the interface when the layer must be handled uniformly (accept it in APIs, return it from constructors) and the embedded struct only for shared state and helpers, keeping the interface small and consumer-defined.
pitfalls: Embedding promotes methods but creates no subtype relationship: a *User is not assignable to *base, and value vs pointer receivers decide which types satisfy the interface.
There is no virtual dispatch: a method redeclared on the outer type shadows the embedded one, so calls through an interface value never reach the embedded implementation for that type.
Conformance is structural, so widening the layer interface silently breaks every type that no longer satisfies it - and large interfaces can be satisfied by accident.
